nameStory: Hyalotheca gets its name from Greek words meaning 'glass case,' referring to how these tiny algae look like they're enclosed in crystal-clear containers. The species name 'dissiliens' means 'bursting apart,' describing how the chain-like colonies break apart when disturbed.
description: Hyalotheca dissiliens is a microscopic freshwater green alga that forms delicate, chain-like colonies floating in ponds and slow streams. Each individual cell looks like a tiny green barrel or cylinder, about 1/100th of an inch long, connected end-to-end with its neighbors. The chains can stretch several inches long and appear as thin, greenish threads in the water. While invisible to the naked eye individually, colonies often create visible green films or mats in quiet waters.

idTips.label: Chain formation
idTips.description: Forms long, straight chains of cylindrical cells connected end-to-end, like microscopic green sausage links that easily break apart when the water is disturbed

idTips.label: Cell shape
idTips.description: Individual cells are barrel-shaped or cylindrical with slightly constricted waists, giving them a distinctive segmented appearance under magnification

idTips.label: Green coloration
idTips.description: Bright green color from chloroplasts arranged in ribbon-like bands that spiral around inside each cell

idTips.label: Transparent sheath
idTips.description: Entire chain enclosed in a clear, jelly-like coating that makes the colony feel slippery and mucilaginous when touched

idTips.label: Fragile connections
idTips.description: Chains break easily into shorter segments when water is stirred, with broken ends clearly visible under a hand lens

habitat: Found in quiet, nutrient-rich freshwater environments throughout New England, including shallow pond edges, slow-moving streams, and temporary pools. Prefers slightly acidic to neutral water with good sunlight penetration. Often grows mixed with other filamentous algae in areas where organic matter accumulates.

seasonality.spring: Colonies begin forming as water warms, appearing as faint greenish films in shallow, sunny areas of ponds and streams.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with most abundant and longest chains visible, often forming noticeable green mats in quiet backwaters.
seasonality.fall: Colonies start breaking down as temperatures drop, with shorter chain fragments more common than long continuous filaments.
seasonality.winter: Largely dormant with minimal visible growth, persisting mainly as individual cells or very short chain segments.

funFact: These tiny algae are actually distant relatives of land plants - they're part of the same evolutionary group that eventually crawled out of the water to become trees, flowers, and grass over 450 million years ago!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other filamentous green algae like Spirogyra or Zygnema, but Hyalotheca's barrel-shaped cells in straight chains are distinctive - think 'green chain links' rather than the long tubular cells of Spirogyra or the star-shaped chloroplasts of Zygnema.
contextualKnowledge: **Uncertain claim flagged**: While desmid algae like Hyalotheca are well-documented, specific details about H. dissiliens distribution and abundance in New England waters may vary from the information provided here, as microscopic algae surveys are limited.
compareHints: Hyalotheca dissiliens differs from its close relative H. mucosa primarily in the thickness and consistency of the mucilaginous sheath surrounding the chains - dissiliens has a thinner, less prominent coating. The cells of dissiliens also tend to be slightly more constricted at their connection points, giving the chains a more segmented appearance than the smoother chains of H. mucosa.
